strengths: Originality: SHINE offers a moderately novel and well-motivated combination of backbone-derived memory states, Meta-LoRA, and an axial row/column-attention Transformer that directly reshapes its outputs into adapters. Bidirectional communication across backbone layers is an interesting distinction from causal layer-wise generators.

Significance: Instant conversion of a roughly 1,150-token context into a reusable LoRA is potentially valuable when the same context serves many queries. The reported 0.3-second adaptation time and removal of the context from subsequent inference suggest a useful amortization regime.

Soundness: The empirical scope is broad, covering reconstruction, completion, multi-turn QA, six standard QA benchmarks, long-context SQuAD variants, multi-hop QA, and scaling experiments. SHINE consistently improves substantially over the context-free baseline and usually outperforms the reported Generative Adapter results.

The paper includes useful architectural and computational detail: tensor shapes, objectives, FLOP and memory derivations, dataset-construction prompts, and an ablation of coupled attention. The MS MARCO MQA construction also includes automatic grounding validation and preserved source splits.
Presentation is generally clear. The architecture diagrams, staged training description, and separation of amortizable adaptation cost from inference cost make the central idea easy to understand.
weaknesses: Soundness: The most important comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. The test-time-training results are imported from another paper using Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, whereas SHINE uses Qwen3-8B; therefore Table 3 cannot support the claim that SHINE defeats SEAL or PaST. The Generative Adapter comparison likewise lacks implementation, backbone, training-data, and tuning details.

The SFT baseline is underspecified and unexpectedly weak: it is trained for 10 epochs on five conversations per context, but the optimizer, learning rate, example construction, stopping criterion, and precise train/test division among questions are absent. Consequently, the claimed advantage over conventional adaptation is not yet convincing.

The main QA evaluation omits uncertainty estimates, multiple seeds, statistical tests, exact decoding and normalization settings, prompts, and per-dataset evaluation sample counts. These omissions are particularly consequential where differences are small and where SHINE surprisingly exceeds a same-backbone model that directly sees the complete context.

Training includes the same named benchmark families used for evaluation—SQuAD, both MS MARCO versions, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultihopQA—but the manuscript does not precisely document split-level deduplication or contamination checks. Preserving MS MARCO splits is stated for the synthetic MQA data, but comparable assurances are missing for the complete training mixture.

The scalability evidence is too weak for the title and central claims. Figure 8 merely shows that larger pretrained backbones obtain lower reconstruction perplexity, without compute-matched training or downstream evaluation. Table 4 varies several factors across configurations, evaluates only 40% of pretraining, and provides no evidence about substantially longer contexts or models beyond 8B.

The characterization as a relatively small, lightweight hypernetwork is misleading without explicit counts. Equation 45 implies roughly (4/36 + 256/4096)P, about 17% of an 8B backbone or approximately 1.4B trainable parameters, while the 36x148x4096 memory tensor contains about 22 million values per example. Actual trainable parameters, training FLOPs, wall-clock time, peak training memory, and adapter storage should be reported.

Claims of being “bottleneck-free” and having superior expressive power are asserted mainly from dimensionality and qualitative architectural arguments. Equal input/output dimensionality does not establish absence of an information or functional bottleneck, and there is no controlled ablation against causal layer-wise generation or a parameter-matched alternative.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The purported code link is malformed (“available a”), and essential details are missing: exact model checkpoint, LoRA target modules and scaling, batch size or accumulation, precision, optimizer parameters, warmup schedule, training steps and duration, dataset mixture sizes, filtering, seeds, QA prompts, and baseline configurations. There is also a notation error in parameter generation, using rR where rO is required.

Presentation sometimes overstates results. SHINE is well below in-context prompting on SQuAD and long-context SQuAD and averages 55.6 versus 69.4 on MS MARCO MQA, so broad claims of parity, outstanding performance, and practical deployment need qualification. The completion objective also cannot literally retain unseen truncated text; it measures prediction rather than storage of that suffix.

Limitations and ethics are not treated appropriately. There is no dedicated limitations analysis, and the impact statement dismisses specific consequences despite a mechanism designed to encode arbitrary text into persistent weights. Privacy leakage, memorization or extraction of sensitive and copyrighted material, deletion and provenance, malicious-context poisoning, adapter sharing, and biases introduced by Qwen-generated QA data all warrant evaluation or mitigation.

strengths: The central architecture is interesting and reasonably original: SHINE reuses the frozen LLM to extract layerwise memory states, then applies alternating token- and layer-axis attention to generate LoRA parameters without per-context gradient updates.
The proposed use case is potentially significant. Converting a context into a reusable adapter could reduce repeated context-prefill costs when many queries share the same document.

The manuscript gives a clear high-level description, helpful diagrams, objective functions, dataset-generation prompts, and analytical compute/memory formulas. Results cover reconstruction, conversational QA, single- and multi-hop QA, and limited scaling studies.

The reported results show that generated adapters contain useful contextual information: SHINE substantially improves over the no-context baseline and usually outperforms the cited Generative Adapter results.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not support the broad claims of mapping arbitrary or diverse contexts. Every principal QA benchmark in Table 2—SQuAD, MS MARCO, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultihopQA—is also listed as instruction-tuning data. Thus, the evidence primarily demonstrates held-out-example performance within trained dataset distributions, not transfer to unseen tasks, domains, or context types.

Several headline comparisons are materially confounded. The test-time-training results are copied from another paper using Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, whereas SHINE uses Qwen3-8B and is instruction-tuned on SQuAD itself. Table 3 therefore cannot establish superiority over SEAL or PaST. The per-context SFT baseline receives only five conversations, while SHINE benefits from extensive meta-training and in-distribution QA tuning, making the comparison difficult to interpret.

The paper overstates performance relative to in-context prompting. In Table 2, SHINE trails in-context prompting by 23.2 F1 on SQuAD, 9.7 on HotpotQA, 7.8 on MuSiQue, and more than 31 points on the long-context SQuAD variants. The claim of general parity is therefore unsupported, even though SHINE is competitive on MS MARCO and 2WikiMultihopQA.

Important architectural claims lack controlled evidence. There is no downstream ablation of the M2P transformer, bidirectional layer communication, memory-token count, pretraining objectives, or post-layer normalization against well-matched alternatives. The half-data experiments test data volume rather than the proposed architectural innovations. Equal input/output dimensionality also does not by itself establish that the system is “bottleneck-free.”

The scalability evidence is weak. Comparing early pretraining perplexity across differently sized backbones mostly shows that larger language models perform better. Table 4 changes multiple quantities across configurations and reports only reconstruction perplexity at 40% of training, not final QA utility, cost-normalized scaling, or saturation. This is insufficient for the repeated claims of strong scaling potential and no capacity saturation.

Efficiency accounting is incomplete and occasionally inconsistent. Equation 21 states that the vocabulary projection is applied only at the final token during language-model training, while Equation 33 correctly charges it at all context positions. Reported memory excludes model and hypernetwork parameters, generated-adapter storage, and training memory. The “negligible” or “no training overhead” language ignores 6B-token meta-training and a hypernetwork whose own approximation implies roughly 17% of the 8B backbone—about 1.4B trainable parameters. Timing results lack batch size, precision, variance, and a sufficiently detailed protocol.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite some useful appendix material. The claimed code link is missing, and the paper omits exact parameter counts, batch sizes, gradient accumulation, weight decay, random seeds, decoding settings, evaluation sample counts, dataset mixture sizes, split-processing details, and baseline implementation details. No uncertainty estimates or repeated runs are reported.

MS MARCO MQA is generated and validated by variants of the same model family without human auditing or analysis of artifacts. Because it supplies 76% of MQA training and is also the main conversational test bed, generator-specific patterns may inflate results. More generally, contamination from the pretrained backbone is not investigated for these established benchmarks.

Presentation is understandable at the conceptual level but contains numerous imprecise or promotional statements, grammatical problems, and notation errors, including the undefined R in the LoRA reshape expression. Claims such as “all [prior methods] are defeated” and “outstanding results” are not appropriate given the unmatched comparisons and large deficits to in-context prompting.

There is no substantive limitations section. The impact statement dismisses potential consequences despite the demonstrated ability to reconstruct text from adapters. Privacy leakage, memorization of sensitive or copyrighted contexts, adapter extraction or sharing, malicious-context behavior, and deletion or revocation of encoded information all merit discussion and evaluation. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evidence and reporting are not reliable enough to justify acceptance.

strengths: Originality: SHINE presents a compelling architecture that reuses the frozen LLM for context encoding and applies alternating layer-wise/token-wise attention to generate LoRAs for all layers. This is a meaningful advance over narrower or more bottlenecked hypernetwork designs.

Significance: Converting a context into a reusable adapter in one forward pass could be valuable when the same information supports many subsequent queries, avoiding repeated context processing and iterative test-time optimization.

Soundness: The evaluation covers multi-turn, single-hop, multi-hop, and long-context QA. SHINE substantially outperforms Generative Adapter on 8 of the 9 reported Table 2 settings and improves markedly over the paper's SFT baseline on MS MARCO MQA (55.6 versus 33.0 F1).

The efficiency results support the basic premise: the reported adapter-generation time is 0.3 seconds versus 29.3 seconds for per-context SFT, while downstream generation avoids repeatedly processing the original context.
The pretraining and instruction-tuning pipeline is sensible, and the synthetic MS MARCO MQA construction is documented with generation and validation prompts, split sizes, and dataset composition.

The paper includes useful partial ablations: half-data variants generally underperform the full model, larger backbones improve validation perplexity, and increased M2P depth or LoRA ranks can improve pretraining performance.
Presentation: The method and data flow are generally easy to follow, with helpful architecture diagrams, equations, efficiency derivations, and appendices.
weaknesses: Soundness: Several conclusions overstate the results. SHINE is well below in-context prompting on SQuAD (63.6 versus 86.8), HotpotQA (59.0 versus 68.7), MuSiQue (28.5 versus 36.3), and especially SQuAD-2K (37.5 versus 84.9). The claim of general parity with in-context learning is therefore not supported, and performance deteriorates sharply as contexts lengthen.

The central architectural attribution is insufficiently ablated. There is no controlled downstream comparison removing bidirectional layer communication, using only the final LLM layer, replacing alternating attention with a simpler projector, varying memory-token count independently, or omitting reconstruction/completion pretraining. Table 4 also changes multiple factors between some rows, so it does not isolate their effects.

Claims about mapping “any meaningful context,” complex reasoning, and scalability exceed the evidence. Evaluation is confined to QA datasets closely aligned with instruction-tuning data, contexts are limited to approximately 1,150 tokens during the main training setup, and there is no evaluation on genuinely new domains, contradictory facts, non-QA tasks, or substantially longer contexts.

The multi-hop results do not establish that the adapters encode semantic structure or reasoning: answer F1 alone cannot distinguish reasoning from memorization or shortcut exploitation, and no supporting-path, counterfactual, or compositional analysis is provided.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. The SFT baseline is trained on only five conversations per context under a particular ten-epoch recipe, without a tuning study. The TTT comparison imports results from a different paper and backbone/training setup, so Table 3 is not a controlled head-to-head comparison. Important alternatives such as compressed/gist-context inference are discussed but not empirically compared.

The efficiency accounting is incomplete for deployment claims. Appendix B.6 reports extra activation memory rather than total memory, while the sizable hypernetwork, generated-adapter storage, adapter transfer or merging, and switching costs are not fully included. From the paper's own approximation, the trainable hypernetwork may be on the order of a billion parameters, yet its exact parameter count and training compute are not reported.

Reproducibility is below the standard expected for a 6B-token training study. The manuscript contains a malformed code-availability placeholder, and it omits exact batch sizes, gradient accumulation, training-step counts for the full stages, optimizer details beyond learning rate, precision, random seeds, variance or confidence intervals, and complete baseline implementation settings. The constructed MS MARCO MQA data is not supplied in the manuscript.

Using Qwen-Flash both to generate and validate MS MARCO MQA does not provide independent quality control. No human audit or measured annotation error is reported, and possible overlap between MS MARCO versions or other training and evaluation collections is not analyzed.

Presentation has avoidable errors and imprecision, including the missing code URL, notation inconsistencies in parameter generation, and promotional statements such as “all of them are defeated.” A dedicated limitations section is absent despite important restrictions involving context length, amortization assumptions, backbone specificity, and in-domain evaluation.

Ethics and limitations are treated too superficially. The generic impact statement does not discuss privacy or copyright leakage from parameterized contexts, extraction attacks, malicious generated adapters, cross-context interference, or safeguards for sensitive information. These issues are material to the proposed deployment scenario, although they do not by themselves invalidate the technical contribution.

strengths: Originality: SHINE presents an interesting context-to-LoRA architecture that reuses frozen-LLM hidden states and applies alternating layer-wise and token-wise attention. This is a plausible way to coordinate adapter parameters across layers while avoiding full attention over all memory states.

Soundness: The method is described with equations and architectural diagrams, and the main experiments cover reconstruction, multi-turn QA, single-hop and multi-hop QA, long-context tasks, and several architecture variants.

Significance: Instant conversion of repeatedly queried context into an adapter is potentially useful when its one-time generation cost can be amortized over many queries. The reported 0.3-second adaptation time is promising relative to per-context fine-tuning.
The reported QA results are substantially above the no-context baseline and usually above Generative Adapter; the multi-hop results suggest that the adapters retain more than isolated surface facts.

Presentation: The paper is generally readable and visually well organized. It provides dataset-construction prompts, FLOP derivations, synthetic-data validation procedures, and some candid negative results, including weaker long-context and GSM8K performance.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central comparison to per-context SFT is not fair evidence of overall adaptation efficiency. SHINE benefits from 6B-token pretraining, large instruction-tuning collections, and roughly 1.4B trainable hypernetwork parameters under the paper's own approximation, whereas the SFT baseline receives only five conversations per context. Training cost, model-resident memory, and the break-even number of downstream queries are not reported.

The claims of parity with in-context learning and superior TTT performance are overstated. In Table 2, SHINE trails in-context prompting by 23.2 F1 on SQuAD, 9.7 on HotpotQA, and 7.8 on MuSiQue, among other gaps. The TTT numbers are imported from another paper using a different Qwen generation and training regime, so Table 3 is not a controlled comparison.

The efficiency accounting omits important deployment costs. Generated adapters contain tens of millions of values and the hypernetwork itself is very large, yet storage, model-parameter memory, adapter switching/merging, and LoRA inference operations are excluded. Calling the method compression is also questionable: the adapter can occupy far more bytes than the original text, even if it avoids repeatedly processing context tokens.

Evaluation contamination and generalization are insufficiently controlled. The 1QA training collection includes SQuAD, MS MARCO, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultiHopQA, which are also the principal evaluation benchmarks. The manuscript does not precisely document split-level deduplication, cross-dataset overlap checks, or contamination from the 6B-token pretraining corpus. MS MARCO MQA evaluation additionally uses synthetic questions and answers generated and validated by the same unspecified Qwen-Flash system used for training data.

The closest context-to-adapter methods are not evaluated adequately. Only Generative Adapter receives a downstream comparison; contemporaneous methods such as Doc-to-LoRA are discussed but not compared. Assertions that MLP or convolutional alternatives lack expressive power are largely qualitative.

The ablations mainly measure pretraining perplexity rather than downstream QA and do not isolate the contributions of pretraining, instruction tuning, bidirectional layer attention, memory-state collection, or parameter-count increases under matched compute. Consequently, the proposed architectural explanation for the gains is not established.

Significance and scalability claims exceed the evidence. The primary model accepts only 1,150 context tokens. SHINE-R is under-specified, trails in-context baselines substantially on nearly every LongBench task, and permits adapter size to grow linearly with context length. Scaling experiments use validation perplexity at only 40% of pretraining and do not demonstrate downstream scaling, compute efficiency, or absence of saturation.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the paper's statement that code is available: the manuscript contains only a broken placeholder link. It omits batch sizes, weight decay, warmup configuration, random seeds, decoding settings, complete prompts, hardware timing protocol, exact dataset preprocessing and mixture counts, checkpoint details, and uncertainty over multiple runs.

Presentation contains consequential overclaiming and some technical ambiguity. For example, 'any meaningful context,' 'negligible overhead,' and 'practical deployment' are unsupported by the restricted QA-focused experiments; the row-attention indexing in Equation 8 is unclear; and no statistical variability is reported.

Ethics and limitations are treated inadequately. The impact statement dismisses all specific consequences despite obvious risks involving private-context memorization, adapter extraction, malicious or poisoned contexts, copyright, and unintended persistence of sensitive information. The limitations are scattered and do not examine these failure modes or the resource cost of training the large hypernetwork.

strengths: Originality/significance: SHINE presents a clear and potentially useful direction—amortizing context adaptation into a single hypernetwork pass—and its alternating layer/token attention is a plausible architectural contribution beyond prior projection-based hypernetworks.

Soundness: The core architecture and two-stage reconstruction/completion plus QA training objectives are described coherently, with useful ablations showing that Transformer processing and access to representations from all backbone layers improve pretraining perplexity.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates single-hop, multi-hop, conversational, long-context, and multitask settings. Several results are promising, including 55.6 F1 versus 33.0 for the chosen SFT baseline on MS MARCO MQA and improvements over Generative Adapter on most reported QA benchmarks.

Presentation: The main data flow is understandable, and the diagrams, equations, computational derivations, dataset-generation prompts, and appendix analyses make the proposed system relatively easy to follow.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. SHINE remains far below direct in-context access on major results—for example, 55.6 versus 69.4 F1 on MS MARCO MQA and 63.6 versus 86.8 on SQuAD—yet the paper repeatedly describes performance as comparable or at parity. On LongBench, SHINE-R trails in-context inference on every dataset, often by a large margin.

Soundness/comparison fairness: The SFT baseline receives only five conversations per context for ten epochs, whereas SHINE benefits from 6B pretraining tokens and hundreds of thousands of instruction examples. This comparison supports fast per-context adaptation under one particular data allocation, but not the broader claim that SHINE is superior to fine-tuning. The substantial one-time cost of training and storing the roughly billion-parameter hypernetwork is omitted from the efficiency narrative.

Soundness/originality: Experimental comparison to the closest contemporaneous context-to-LoRA method, Doc-to-LoRA, is absent despite its citation. Only Generative Adapter is evaluated among hypernetworks; Text-to-LoRA, compositional adapters, and Drag-and-Drop are dismissed largely through qualitative assertions that Transformers are more expressive. Consequently, the claimed state of the art and architectural advantage are not established.

Methodological support: Claims such as “bottleneck-free,” backpropagation-like information flow, and superior expressive power are intuitive rather than theoretically demonstrated. Appendix C's own approximation gives about (4/36 + 256/4096)P, or roughly 1.4B trainable parameters for an 8B backbone, which makes “a relatively small number of parameters” misleading. The rank-8 generated LoRA remains an explicit functional bottleneck.

Evaluation validity: The broad multitask evidence is weak because Table 11 applies SQuAD-style token F1 to dialogue, personality-conditioned generation, summarization, and GSM8K instead of task-standard metrics such as ROUGE or exact match. SHINE also drops from 44.48 to 25.27 on GSM8K relative to in-context inference, undermining the general adaptation narrative.

Efficiency analysis contains questionable accounting. The no-KV “peak generation memory” formulas multiply activation and attention storage by the number of layers, although inference normally releases layer-local activations rather than retaining them across all layers. Generation FLOPs are presented per decoding step while empirical generation covers whole responses. No measured VRAM or FLOP validation is supplied, weakening a central efficiency claim.

Statistical evidence is inadequate: results appear to come from single runs, with no seeds, confidence intervals, variance, significance tests, or sample counts attached to the main benchmark tables. Scaling conclusions are based mainly on validation perplexity after 40% of pretraining and a small number of configurations, rather than downstream performance or compute-matched scaling studies.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the scale of the claims. The manuscript's code-availability statement contains only a placeholder, and it omits batch size, gradient accumulation, precision, optimizer coefficients, weight decay, warmup schedule, decoding settings, checkpoint-selection rules, total training time, and exact mixture/preprocessing details. The new 366K-example MS MARCO MQA dataset has no stated release location or license and depends on an insufficiently specified Qwen-Flash generation and validation service.

Presentation: The prose is readable but frequently promotional (“outstanding,” “defeated by SHINE,” “strictly more challenging”) and sometimes substitutes assertions for controlled evidence. There is no dedicated limitations discussion despite clear restrictions including the 1,150-token base setting, degraded multi-turn behavior, poor reasoning transfer, reliance on synthetic QA, and weaker long-context performance.

Ethics: The impact statement dismisses all specific concerns, even though the method is explicitly trained to reproduce contexts verbatim in persistent weights. The paper does not discuss privacy or copyright leakage, deletion and provenance of encoded data, malicious-context poisoning, safety-behavior modification by generated adapters, or auditing of the synthetic dataset. These are material deployment risks for the claimed context-to-parameter conversion capability.

strengths: Originality: SHINE offers a novel and well-motivated context-to-LoRA design. Reusing frozen LLM representations from every layer and applying alternating layer/token attention provides a plausible way to generate coordinated adapters without a narrow projection bottleneck.

Soundness: The core empirical result is promising. On nine QA settings, SHINE consistently beats the context-free baseline and usually outperforms Generative Adapter, with especially strong results on MS MARCO and 2WikiMultihopQA. The multi-turn, long-context, and reconstruction experiments provide complementary evidence that useful contextual information reaches the generated weights.

Significance: Producing reusable adapters in one forward pass could be valuable when a context supports many later queries. The reported 0.3-second adapter-generation time versus tens of seconds for per-context fine-tuning illustrates the practical appeal.

The ablations support several design choices: Transformer mappings substantially outperform linear alternatives, using representations from all backbone layers helps, and larger backbones, LoRA ranks, and M2P depth improve pretraining perplexity.

Presentation: The main architecture and two-stage training pipeline are explained clearly with equations and diagrams. The appendix contains useful FLOP derivations, dataset-construction prompts, additional SFT baselines, and architectural comparisons.

The paper discusses genuine limitations, including degradation with longer conversations, poorer conversion of long or low-quality text, weak GSM8K performance, and SHINE-R's remaining gap to in-context inference.
weaknesses: Soundness: The main supervised evaluation is insufficiently controlled. The instruction-tuning collection explicitly includes SQuAD, MS MARCO, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, and 2WikiMultihopQA, which are also the evaluation benchmarks. Although test or validation splits are mentioned, the paper does not clearly document split-level deduplication, context overlap checks, or whether every baseline receives comparable benchmark-specific meta-training. This weakens claims about mapping arbitrary contexts and cross-task generalization.

Several comparisons are not apples-to-apples. SHINE benefits from 6B-token pretraining plus large-scale instruction tuning, whereas the per-context SFT baselines train on only a handful of conversations. The test-time-training numbers are copied from another study using Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct rather than the paper's Qwen3-8B setup. These results demonstrate different operational tradeoffs, but do not establish unqualified superiority.

The efficiency accounting favors SHINE in some respects: in-context context-prefill is assigned zero amortizable cost, even though its KV cache can be computed once and reused for multiple questions. End-to-end throughput, break-even query counts, adapter storage, and the approximately 1.4B trainable hypernetwork parameters implied by Equation 45 are not reported clearly.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims. Missing details include batch sizes, training compute and duration, optimizer parameters beyond peak learning rates, warmup settings, decoding parameters, random seeds or uncertainty estimates, exact dataset mixture sizes, M2P attention configuration, LoRA target modules/scaling, and timing methodology. The manuscript's code link is also incomplete in the provided version.

The experiments report essentially single-run point estimates. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, human checks of generated MS MARCO MQA beyond validation by the same model family, or systematic robustness tests for contradictory, adversarial, out-of-distribution, or irrelevant contexts.

Some conclusions are overstated. SHINE remains substantially below direct in-context access on six of nine principal QA columns and most LongBench tasks; reconstruction of familiar-domain text does not by itself show semantic knowledge internalization; and finite scaling curves at 40% of training are insufficient to conclude that there is no capacity saturation.

The long-context extension is preliminary: its adapter size grows linearly with context length, it is evaluated on only six LongBench tasks, and it lacks matched latency, storage, and quality comparisons against retrieval, context compression, or reusable KV-cache baselines.

Presentation and ethics: prose occasionally becomes promotional, and the impact statement dismisses domain-specific consequences. Context-to-weight conversion raises privacy leakage, memorization, deletion, malicious-context, and adapter-sharing risks that deserve analysis, even if they are not presently grounds for rejection.
